item.title: Rardin Didn’t Ask, Didn’t Know: City Leaders Cast Doubt on Downtown Projects Without Checking First
item.description:
Alamogordo N. M- Two downtown business owners say they were publicly attacked at the most recent Alamogordo City Commission meeting by a commissioner who never contacted them, has never visited their properties and does not represent their district. They say his remarks were wrong, damaging and defamatory. Former City Manager Dr. Hernandez, who recommended both projects, is also disputing how the meeting described them.

The owners of the White Sands Theater and Rad Retrocade have each received Local Economic Development Act (LEDA) funding. Both told Alamogordo Town News that their projects are moving forward and that they are in full compliance with their agreements with the city. According to Hernandez, each owner plans to put more than $1 million of their own money into their building. The owners say what they got in return was a public suggestion from the dais that they had taken the city’s money and done nothing.

The exchange

The discussion came up under an agenda item on allocating the city’s remaining LEDA funds. Commissioner Josh Rardin pointed to the two projects.

https://youtube.com/shorts/9fvl_hPLwIU?is=m-rWi59pnBAZk8eu

“The ones down there on New York Avenue we gave money to, I haven’t seen any action on either of them,” Rardin said.“In the event that they don’t do anything with them, what is our recourse? Do we call that back or…”

City Manager Robert Stockwell did not correct the premise. He went further. “Well, we can try,” he said, adding that it“baffled” him that the city would “give a million dollars to somebody before there’s bills to pay.” He said “the White Sands Theater got a million dollar check. We don’t know where that money is.” The discussion then raised the possibility that there would be “nothing to claw back” and that the city could end up with “one more derelict building.”The two downtown projects were discussed in the same breath as Sunbaked Biscuits, which Stockwell described as a complete default on a $1.9 million project.

No one at the meeting offered any evidence that either downtown project had stalled or broken its agreement. According to the owners, no one had asked them.

Former city manager: “inaccurate”

Hernandez was city manager when both LEDA agreements were approved. In a statement, Hernandez said they were“deeply disappointed by the Commission meeting’s characterization of downtown revitalization.”

“The claim that funding was provided without bills having been paid is inaccurate. So is the claim that nothing is happening downtown,” Hernandez said. “Troy and Alex submitted invoices and status updates, with plans involving more than $1 million of their own investment in each building.”

Hernandez also confirmed what both owners told Alamogordo Town News: no one at the meeting had talked to them first. “To my knowledge, only the mayor and I have reached out to them,” Hernandez said. “Public funding deserves scrutiny. That scrutiny requires accurate information and direct communication.”

Hernandez noted that the projects were the commission’s decision, not a city manager acting alone. “I only recommended; the Commission approved. It is no secret the Commissioners were willing to push back when they disagreed. But both were approved unanimously. I stand by my recommendations.”

The agreements were drafted under Hernandez and the city attorney at the time, using the state’s LEDA template, as the state recommends.

“The approach is the same. The location is different.”

Hernandez also pointed out a contradiction. Stockwell has been promoting creative public-private partnerships to deal with deteriorating properties on 10th Street. That is the same strategy, Hernandez said, that the city used downtown.

“Mr. Stockwell’s proposed solutions for 10th Street, addressing deteriorating properties through creative public-private partnerships, are exactly what we pursued downtown. The approach is the same. The location is different,” Hernandez said.

“I agree that 10th Street needs attention. Downtown did too. Perhaps its beauty today makes its former condition easy to forget. Mr. Stockwell may not have seen it then, or have all the correct information, but the Commission did.”Hernandez said those conditions led the commission to approve the downtown Metropolitan Redevelopment Area (MRA) in 2019 and to back its redevelopment.

That effort combined state grants, city investment, MainStreet partnerships and private investment from businesses including Ink Well, Rad Retrocade, the White Sands Theater and Pymo.

“Different priorities are understandable,” Hernandez said.“Praising an approach for 10th Street while disparaging that same approach downtown is unfortunate. Casting doubt on the business owners who invested significantly here undermines the very partnerships the City Manager now says it wants to build.”

“Uninformed”

When Alamogordo Town News contacted Stockwell after the meeting, he acknowledged he was “uninformed of the status of the two properties.” He said he had been trying to explain to the commission that the city’s options would be limited if a project ever failed, because the agreements have limited reporting requirements, and that he did not like the contracts.

That leaves a public discussion of possible clawbacks against two local businesses, held by a city manager who says he did not know the status of their projects and a commissioner who, according to both owners, never picked up the phone. Meanwhile, the former city manager says the invoices and status updates had already been submitted.

Not his district, and no phone call

Neither property is in Rardin’s district. Both owners told Alamogordo Town News that Rardin made no attempt to call, meet with or visit them before he spoke at the meeting. They said neither Rardin nor Stockwell has ever asked for a walkthrough or a progress update.

Rardin has described himself as a contractor. Anyone in construction knows that the early stages of a major renovation, such as roofing, demolition, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, security and architectural design, happen mostly out of sight. A building that looks unchanged from the sidewalk is not a building where nothing is happening.

Rad Retrocade: in compliance, opening spring 2027

Alex, the owner of Rad Retrocade, said he has submitted receipts to the city and met with city engineer Shelly Barron several months ago, and that the project is in full compliance with its agreement.

Extensive work has already been done inside the building, he said. New air conditioning units have been ordered. Significant equipment and arcade games for the mezzanine are in local storage, and work continues on the electrical, plumbing and other systems. More exterior work will be visible starting in December, and the arcade remains on track to open in spring 2027, as promised.

Alex said he was upset by the exchange, which he considers an attack on his business, and has contacted an attorney about the comments.

White Sands Theater: new roof, new wiring and a theft along the way

Troy, the owner of the White Sands Theater, also owns three operating businesses, including the German restaurant on New York Avenue. He told Alamogordo Town News he was angered by the commission’s remarks and has sent a scathing letter to the mayor and city manager. He says the project is in full compliance with its agreement.

The theater’s latest renovation update shows a project that has been working through serious obstacles:

The old fly loft on the roof has been removed, and a new roof is on the building.The back storage room door and window have been sealed with concrete to stop break-ins.Thieves broke in and stole a large portion of the building’s copper electrical wiring.The owners have contracted to upgrade and replace the electrical system to support the theater’s new digital equipment.A contractor hired to redo the exterior stucco took the owners’ deposit and disappeared. A new contractor has been hired, and the owners plan to take legal action to recover the deposit.An architect is designing the interior layout, which will slightly change the building’s footprint.

“Progress takes time, but we can’t wait to show you what’s coming together,” the owners wrote.

What comes next

The city’s first formal check on the LEDA projects is expected in December. Both owners say they welcome it. They want to know why that check-in didn’t happen before their businesses were questioned in a public meeting.

Alamogordo Town News will continue to follow both projects.

item.title: In Memory of Adelin Frances Stokes Schauer
item.description:
Adelin Frances Stokes Schauer, age 94, passed away peacefully at her home in Alamogordo, New Mexico on Thursday, October 8, 2026.

Adelin was born in Carrizozo, New Mexico on August 22, 1932. She cherished her early years growing up on her family's ranch outside of town before moving to Truth or Consequences, New Mexico where she graduated from high school. She went on to attend Texas Tech University, earning a Bachelor of Business Administration degree.

Following college, Adelin moved to Roswell, New Mexico where she met and married William Carl "Bill" Schauer. Together they raised two children, Leda and Tony. The family eventually settled in High Rolls Mountain Park, New Mexico surrounded by tall pine trees, apple orchards, trout ponds, and winter snows.

Following Bill's passing and as her children established their careers, Adelin pursued further education, earning a counseling degree from CBN University. She then dedicated many years to serving the emotional and spiritual needs of her community. Throughout her life, Adelin was a devoted servant leader, serving as the Southern New Mexico Area President of Women’s Aglow Fellowship, President of Alamogordo Republican Women, and sharing her musical talents as an organist and pianist while teaching Sunday school at various churches.

item.title: PNM sale clears a hurdle as regulators pass on Zimmer stock probe
item.description:
The fight over who will own the company that keeps the lights on for most of the Albuquerque metro area is headed back into the hearing room.

On Friday, Oct. 16, hearing examiners for the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission declined to open an investigation into a roughly $200 million sale of TXNM Energy stock to New York investment firm Zimmer Partners. In a second order the same day, they allowed TXNM — the Albuquerque-based parent of Public Service Company of New Mexico — and Blackstone Infrastructure to refile their acquisition application with richer customer benefits and paperwork showing that an earlier, illegal stock sale between the two companies has been unwound.

Taken together, the rulings remove the last procedural obstacle that had stalled the case since summer. The PRC is scheduled to hold a status conference this week to set a calendar for a weeklong hearing on whether the $11.5 billion deal serves the public interest.

For the roughly 550,000 PNM customers in Albuquerque, Rio Rancho, Santa Fe, Las Cruces and other communities, the outcome will determine whether New Mexico's largest electric utility passes from public shareholders into the hands of one of the world's biggest private equity firms.

The Zimmer question grew out of a ruling that rattled the deal in July.

On the same day Blackstone and TXNM signed their merger agreement in May 2025, a Blackstone holding company bought 8 million newly issued TXNM shares for about $400 million, giving it a 7.59% stake. Albuquerque nonprofit Prosperity Works challenged the purchase, arguing state law bars anyone from taking a stake in a utility for the purpose of an acquisition without the commission's prior approval.

Hearing examiners agreed in June, and on July 2 the commission voted 2-1 to order the sale reversed. Commissioners Pat O'Connell and Gabriel Aguilera formed the majority; Commissioner Greg Nibert dissented, warning that forcing the companies to repay the money would strain TXNM's finances and, in turn, its ratepayers. The order fined TXNM $100,000 and Blackstone affiliates $200,000.

"You've got to follow the law or else the regulatory compact doesn't work," O'Connell said at the time.

Weeks after the Blackstone purchase, in June 2025, TXNM sold about 3.6 million shares — roughly $200 million worth — to Zimmer Partners and affiliated funds. Like the Blackstone agreement, the Zimmer contract committed the buyer to vote its shares in favor of the merger. Santa Fe-based New Energy Economy and the New Mexico Consumer Protection Alliance argued that made the Zimmer sale another piece of the same financing structure and asked the PRC to investigate it, too.

The examiners disagreed, calling the Zimmer deal "fundamentally different." They found no comparable evidence that Zimmer took part in the acquisition process or bought shares as part of a merger. A PRC spokesperson, Patrick Rodriguez, said the firm acted on its own, had no ties to Blackstone and bought its shares only after the merger agreement had been signed. TXNM had previously described Zimmer as a longtime investor in the company.

New Energy Economy executive director Mariel Nanasi called the voting language in the Zimmer contract "damning evidence," but said she understood the examiners' reasoning and argued the request had been worth making.

The second order is the one with direct consequences for monthly bills.

When the companies first filed in August 2025, they offered a $105 million rate credit spread over four years — about $3.51 a month, or roughly $168 total, for an average residential customer — plus $10 million for PNM's Good Neighbor Fund and $60 million for economic development and energy transition programs. Critics, led by New Energy Economy, dismissed the credits as too small and noted the package lacked a rate freeze, a common feature of utility takeovers.

In September, TXNM and Blackstone asked permission to revise those terms. The sweetened package now on track for review includes:

The companies have also pledged to hold TXNM for at least 10 years, keep PNM headquartered and managed in New Mexico, and honor existing union contracts with IBEW workers. TXNM said Friday it still believes the sale is the right choice for New Mexico; Blackstone said it was pleased to move forward.

The case has drawn some of the largest public turnouts the PRC has seen. Protesters have rallied repeatedly outside PNM's Downtown Albuquerque headquarters, and public comment sessions — including one at the University of New Mexico Student Union — have been dominated by opponents worried that private equity ownership will push rates higher. At the July hearing, when the commission chair asked the crowd who supported the deal, no one raised a hand. Albuquerque City Councilor Stephanie Telles has spoken against the merger, while a handful of lawmakers, including Rep. Meredith Dixon of Albuquerque, have backed it as an economic development opportunity.

The companies argue Blackstone's capital is needed as PNM races to meet the 2019 Energy Transition Act's goal of carbon-free power by 2040 and to upgrade an aging grid. Opponents counter that a buyer seeking private-equity-scale returns will ultimately recover its investment from ratepayers.

New Mexicans have been here before. In 2021, the PRC unanimously rejected Avangrid's bid for PNM, a decision in which New Energy Economy's opposition played a central role. The current commission — now three appointed members rather than five elected ones — has also already ruled on a private equity utility takeover: it voted 2-1 this year to let Louisiana-based Bernhard Capital Partners buy New Mexico Gas Co. for $1.25 billion. Aguilera dissented in that case, saying the risks outweighed the benefits. That deal included about $22.4 million in rate credits for the gas utility's roughly 553,000 customers — a fraction of what Blackstone is now offering PNM customers.

The PRC accepts public comment on the case by email at public.comment@prc.nm.gov.

item.title: NSF refuses historic listing for Sunspot
item.description:
The National Science Foundation says it will not apply to add Sunspot Solar Observatory to the National Register of Historic Places even though it filled out the paperwork.

“NSF recognizes the historic significance of the observatory and appreciates your interest in its future,” Dr. Linnea Avallone, NSF Chief Officer for Research Facilities, wrote on Wednesday, Oct. 14. “However, after considering the request in the context of NSF’s existing decisions and obligations, NSF does not intend to pursue formal listing of the property on the National Register.”

Avallone’s e-mail was sent to Ricardo St. Hilaire an attorney who specializes in cultural affairs and an avid amateur solar astronomer, in reponse to St. Hilaire’s Oct. 6 “formal request asking NSF to move forward with the National Register of Historic Places nomination for the Sacramento Peak Observatory Historic District. As explained in the request, NSF completed the National Register documentation in February 2020. It is respectfully requested that NSF now take the remaining steps to move the nomination through the federal process.

“Listing Sunspot Solar Observatory/Sacramento Peak Observatory on the National Register provides significant advantages to all stakeholders. For NSF, in particular, listing would provide a recognized framework for managing the historic campus, facilitate potential reuse, build partnerships, and help cultivate options for the property's future disposition.”

Sunspot’s history dates from 1947 when two Air Force observers set up camp with a single telescope at Sacramento Peak to check seeing conditions. Over the next 30 years, Sunspot grew from early space weather forecasting station to a world leader in studying the Sun to understand better how it affects us on Earth. A 1976 change in defense funding forced the Air Force to plan its shut down. But, the NSF responded to the world science community and took over.

In the late 1990s, NSF started planning what is now the 4-meter (13-ft) aperture Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope atop Maui. Its development and operation costs forced NSF to plan “divestment” in hopes that a team would emerge to take over. New Mexico State University had operated the Dunn Solar Telescope for several years until Jan. 6 when a mercury leak in its main bearing forced its shutdown.

During 2016–20, NSF held environmental impact hearings in Alamogordo and then published its final decision of record. Of four alternatives — 1) operations as-is, 2) partnership, 3) mothball while looking for options, and 4) total demolition and remediation — NSF chose 1 and 4.

“As reflected in NSF’s February 2026 update, no parties presented viable plans that provide full financial support for continued observatory operations or assume ownership of the telescope or observatory,” Avallone wrote. “NSF therefore proceeded with implementation of Alternative 4, consistent with the 2019 Record of Decision. It would not be typical for a federal agency to nominate a facility that is slated for demolition to the National Register; in fact, listed properties are typically delisted after such a loss of historic integrity. NSF therefore does not intend to initiate the nomination process.”

NSF also has resisted efforts by Sunspot Community Center and others to implement Alternative 3 for the remainder of the site and allow time to develop a plan and seek funding.

Given this position, it appears likely that NSF plans to proceed with total demolition and remediation, making it difficult for supports to secure any kind of commitment. The current $9,999,334 contract with Thronton Tomasetti to destroy the Dunn — $666 short of the $10 million reporting threshold under the Federal Truth in Negotiations Act — runs Sept. 23, 2026–March 23, 2027. NSF has declined to comment on plans to request proposals or a timetable for the remainder of Sunspot. The previous contracts to remove the mercury and demolish were sole-source, unadvertised, and categorized as “Controlled, unclassified information,” and therefore outside Freedom of Information Act disclosure.

NSF will not let Sunspot be forgotten. It promised $100,000 for an interpretive exhibit. That is about 500 square feet (about 22x22 ft) at quoted average costs of $200/square foot. Meanwhile, it has spent $5 million of a science center at the collapsed Arecibo radio telescope in Puerto Rico and $4.5 million to build a science center inside the decommissioned McMath-Pierce Solar Telescope at Kitt Peak (AZ) National Observatory.

item.title: Sunspot Slated for Demolition and To Be Gone By 2028
item.description:
The Dunn Solar Telescope will be demolished by spring of 2027 and Sunspot Solar Observatory will be gone by Christmas 2027, the National Science Foundation and the U.S. Forest Service announced today.

NSF has also published an unredacted version of the “Justification for Other Than Full and Open Competition” in awarding the demolition contract to Thornton Tomasetti.

The complete schedule for demolition is:

October–December, 2026: Scaffolding constructed around DST; removal of the concrete structure begins from the top down.

January–March 2027: Concrete and interior structures removed; DST demolition to ground level complete; site clean-up and demobilization. Procurement and Phase 1 task order award for Sacramento Peak site demolition. This matches the Sept. 23, 2026–March 23, 2027 time frame for the $10 million contract awarded last month to Thornton Tomasetti.

April–September 2027: Phase 1 implementation, “removing structures that have been unused for extended periods.” Phase 2 contract award.

October–December 2027: Phase 2 “will focus on removal of all other structures on site.”

Work begins with an assessment of other hazardous materials — asbestos, lead-based pain, lead-bearing plumbing, and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB) — that were common construction materials during the 1950s and ‘60s when Sunspot was built and expanded. NSF will work with the New Mexico Environment Department on removal and safe disposal.

“Where feasible, contractors will also work to identify instruments and equipment inside the telescope that can be safely retrieved and decontaminated for continued scientific or educational use,” the NSF stated. This is contrary to an earlier statement that no further instrument removal would be permitted.

ATN has asked NSF for clarification on which structures are involved in the two phases, and whether demolition includes the post office, which is privately owned even though it sits on Federal property, and the fire/EMS station, which belongs to Otero County.

Meanwhile, NSF continues discussions with the Apache Point Observatory about maintaining the water supply

On Sept. 29, NSF reposted the unredacted announcement of the demolition contract “for 30 days to correct inadvertent redactions in the previously posted version.” The major revelation was the estimated total value of $20 million. That is $6.7 million greater than the three awards made to date:

• Original award (3/23/2026,), $310,000, to assess the situation and later increased to $670,679 to cover purchase of long-lead items,• Second award (7/10/2026), $3, 071,489, to remove mercury, and• Third award (9/23/2026), 9,999,334, to demolish the Dunn.

Mike England, NSF head of media affairs, said that what appears to be three separate contracts are “are task orders issued against the same Indefinite Delivery/Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) contract.” No extensions are planned. ATN has asked for clarification on why the estimated value in the initial posting is much higher than the awards posted to date.

This story will be updated when new information is available.

item.title: Former GOP chair hopeful Zac Anaya quits Republican Party two weeks before Election Day
item.description:
RIO RANCHO — Zac Anaya, a Rio Rancho Republican who ran for the Legislature this year and briefly sought the state party chairmanship, announced Monday evening that he has left the Republican Party and will register as an independent.

The announcement lands 15 days before the Nov. 3 general election. It also lands as the Republican Party of New Mexico heads into a post-election leadership vote with no permanent chair, after a year of lawsuits, failed meetings and an open split between its northern and southern wings.

Anaya, 33, made the announcement in a social media post after nearly three weeks without posting videos. "I've given up on the Republican Party of New Mexico," he wrote. "And frankly, I've given up on our statewide government."

Anaya argued that the state GOP has spent years failing to build competitive campaigns, raise money or hold its own leaders accountable. He said the party preaches faith, family and integrity while letting personal grudges, hypocrisy and favoritism consume it.

He did not spare Democrats, blaming decades of one-party rule for the state's struggles with education, poverty, crime and addiction. He also faulted national Republicans for adding trillions to the debt.

Anaya said the fighting had taken a personal toll. He wrote that his wife, two children and faith deserve more of his time than another political argument.

"I am no longer a Republican. I am not a Democrat," he wrote. He said he will stay independent "until one of the parties in New Mexico can figure it out," and urged followers to do the same.

Anaya lost a June primary challenge to state Rep. Joshua Hernandez in House District 60.

Anaya's sharpest line pointed at the governor's race. He wrote that one of the most qualified Republicans to run for governor in a generation is struggling to raise money and compete. He did not name him, but the reference is to Gregg Hull, the GOP nominee and former longtime mayor of Anaya's hometown, Rio Rancho.

The fundraising gap is real. With fewer than three weeks to go, Democrat Deb Haaland was still well ahead in money, according to campaign reports filed Oct. 13. Hull took in about $634,000 from roughly 1,400 donations in the latest period and has raised about $1.5 million for the general election. He spent nearly all of the period's haul.

Hull's campaign says the numbers reflect a focus on in-state donors. Filings show 99% of his donors are New Mexicans. Hull has also cited donor fatigue after the June primary.

In June, Hull said he had no preference in the party's chair fight.

Anaya's exit is the latest fallout from the fight over Amy Barela, the Otero County commissioner who won the party chair in December 2024 with 157 votes to 58 for John Brenna.

The trouble began when Barela filed in March 2026 for reelection to her county commission seat, which drew a primary challenge from Republican Jonathan Emery. Critics said party rules barred a chair from staying in the post while running in a contested primary.

The dispute escalated through the spring. On April 18, Barela's opponents gathered in Belen to replace her. They drew 252 members, short of the 362 needed for a quorum, and passed a nonbinding resolution declaring she had vacated the post. Barela maintained she was still chair.

On April 30, Emery, gubernatorial candidate Duke Rodriguez and lieutenant governor candidate Aubrey Blair Dunn sued. They said Barela and other party officials broke party rules and tilted the primary in favor of preferred candidates.

On May 27, District Judge Cindy Mercer ordered Barela to step down as chair. The ruling also barred top party officials from publicly backing candidates in contested primaries. Days later, on June 2, Emery narrowly defeated Barela in the Otero County Commission primary.

The New Mexico Supreme Court unanimously denied the party's appeal on June 10. Barela announced soon afterward that she would run for chair again.

On June 20, the party convened in Las Cruces to pick a new chair. Only 163 members attended, most from southern counties, and the vote failed for lack of a quorum after many northern Republicans stayed away. Northern Republicans then called a second meeting in Belen for June 27.

The party called Mercer's ruling a violation of free speech. Barela's critics called her a rule breaker. Rodriguez said a small group had long treated the party like a private club.

Anaya entered the chair race in June as one of four challengers to Barela, along with attorney Robert Aragon, Brenna and KKOB radio host Brandon Vogt.

He framed it as a fight between regions. He told Source NM that a Barela win would show that southern New Mexico had bullied its way into the chairmanship. He soon dropped out, reportedly to avoid splitting the anti-Barela vote in the north.

The party enters the election under an interim leader. First Vice Chair Mike Nelson has run the party since Barela's removal and was still issuing statements as interim chair as of Oct. 10. A further chair vote was rescheduled for late July in Albuquerque after the quorum failures, though no result has been reported.

A permanent chair is set to be chosen after the general election. Earlier reporting placed that State Central Committee vote in December, for a full two-year term, with the new chair serving into 2027.

No public forecasts of that race have been published, but several factors are likely to shape it.

Turnout may matter most. Both summer votes collapsed when one faction stayed home, so whichever side can bring a quorum into the room is likely to pick the chair.

The field opposing Barela has also narrowed. Brenna and Vogt were the remaining challengers after Anaya and others stepped aside to consolidate support.

Barela retains a reliable southern base and will leave the county commission in December, freeing her to focus on the party. But she lost her own primary and was ruled against by two courts.

The Nov. 3 results could tip the balance. A poor Republican showing is likely to sharpen calls for new leadership, though Barela has argued since February that the party's problems are structural.

Anaya's departure does not by itself show the Barela wing gaining ground. He was one of her critics, and his post names no leader or faction. His exit removes a voice from the anti-Barela side, not a vote for her.

The split surfaced again Monday, the same day as Anaya's announcement, when President Trump revived his call to rename the state. In a Truth Social post, Trump said New Mexico should immediately change its name to "New America" and claimed the change would add value and prestige. He first floated the idea in September, posting a map with "Mexico" crossed out.

Hull, the party's nominee for governor, rejected the idea Monday night. In a post on X, he said he stands by his earlier position that New Mexico does not need a new name and that the state's identity is "never up for negotiation." He said voters are focused on jobs, taxes and rising costs.

Barela took a different tone. She shared Fox News's post on Trump's proposal on social media with the comment, "Let's make more heads spin!

The contrast put the former chair on the opposite side of the issue from the party's own nominee for governor two weeks before the election. Hull is attempting to unite the state and understands he needs the vote of independents and moderate Democrats.

Barela thrives on division and extremism not wanting to bridge across party lines for a win. 

Democrats seized on the proposal. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham called it a tired bit meant to distract from policy failures, and U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján said the name dates back centuries and will outlast Trump's time in office. A president has no legal power to rename a state.

Voters go to the polls Nov. 3, with every statewide office on the ballot. The State Central Committee then meets to elect a permanent chair.

Months after a court removed her, Barela's influence still shapes the party. The fight over her chairmanship split Republicans along regional lines, stalled two leadership votes and left the party without a permanent leader through the campaign season.

Anaya's departure is one more sign of that fallout and yet another Barela casualty. 

The clearest measure of whether the party's leadership has been effective will come at the polls on Nov. 3. With an open governor's seat, Republicans have a chance to compete against a Democratic nominee they see as vulnerable, even as Haaland holds a wide fundraising lead.

That outcome may decide the chair race as much as anything said in Belen or Las Cruces. A strong night for Hull would strengthen the case that the party can win despite its divisions. 

A loss would hand the next fight for the chairmanship to whoever can best argue that the party needs to change. Stay tuned we will be there.

item.title: Our Youth Have Something to Say. Are We Listening?
item.description:
Thoughts from Dr Stephanie Hernandez former acting city manager city of Alamogordo: 

I walked away from the first meeting of the Mayor's Youth Advisory Commission (MYAC) with a full heart and a renewed sense of optimism about Alamogordo's future.

Although this was an informal meeting intended to establish rules, expectations, and structure, it quickly became something much more meaningful. I had the privilege of watching some incredibly intelligent young minds come together, not to complain about their community, but to figure out how they could make it better.

We started by asking a simple question: What do you hope to gain from participating in MYAC?

Their answers included learning leadership skills, becoming better public speakers, understanding how city government operates, learning how governing bodies make decisions, and finding ways to make a difference.

Then we asked what concerned them about our community.

Two themes immediately emerged: safety and having things to do after school.

As the conversation developed, their concerns became much more specific. They talked about safety for young drivers who are still learning to navigate our streets. They expressed concerns about substance abuse in schools, including what they are seeing and hearing at the middle school level, and the need for serious consequences for individuals who provide these substances to children.

They also talked about something that I found particularly meaningful: the need for safe places where young people can gather, complete homework, socialize, and simply spend time with their peers.

They recognized that not every child goes home to the same environment. Not everyone has a safe, quiet place to study or somewhere they feel comfortable spending time after school.

And they weren't simply asking for another place to hang out. They were already thinking about the obstacles. How would something like that be funded? How do we make existing spaces safer? How do we turn ideas into something realistic?

These are the kinds of questions we should want our young people asking.

What impressed me most was that not one of these students approached the conversation from a selfish perspective. They weren't just asking what the city could do for them personally. They were advocating for their classmates, their peers, younger students, and even people they may never meet.

They came out of the gate thinking about the greater good of Alamogordo.

And that brings me to something I believe is important for everyone to understand about MYAC.

This commission is not about adults telling kids what to do, what to think, or even what issues they should discuss.

It is about giving our young people the opportunity to tell adults what matters to them.

Our role as mentors is to help them understand the processes, provide them with tools, and support them as they develop their ideas. It is not our job to dictate their priorities or steer their conversations toward what we think is important.

With 16 student participants and nine mentors, I believe we have an incredible opportunity to build something meaningful.

But one of the final questions of the meeting is what has stayed with me.

A student asked:

"But how do we get people to listen to us?

That question simultaneously made my heart ache and jump for joy.

It hurt because it reminded me that some of our young people don't feel their voices are being heard. They have concerns. They have ideas. They want to participate. But they are unsure whether the adults making decisions will take them seriously.

And yet, that same question gave me tremendous hope.

Because here was a young person who wasn't asking whether their opinion mattered. They were asking how to make sure it was heard.

That is where leadership begins.

We often talk about our youth as the future of Alamogordo. And they certainly are. But sometimes, in focusing so much on who they will become, we overlook who they already are.

They are our citizens today. They live in our neighborhoods, attend our schools, travel our streets, and experience the consequences of decisions made by adults every single day.

Their voices deserve a place in those conversations.

I am honored to be part of this effort and to work alongside the mentors and students who have committed their time to MYAC.

Our young people have already demonstrated that they are intelligent, thoughtful, compassionate, and willing to tackle difficult issues.

Now comes the responsibility of making sure their ideas aren't simply acknowledged and forgotten.

The question is no longer whether our young people have something meaningful to contribute to Alamogordo. They clearly do.

The question is whether we, as adults, are willing to listen.

After this first meeting, I can say one thing with confidence: Alamogordo's future looks a little brighter to me.

item.title: Mayor's Youth Advisory Commission holds first meeting
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Alamogordo's newest advisory body met for the first time Monday night and its members wasted little time telling city leaders what matters to them.

The Mayor's Youth Advisory Commission (MYAC) gathered for a little over an hour at the Dudley Community Center. The commission includes 16 student participants and nine adult mentors, according to Mayor Sharon McDonald. Youth commissioners and mentors opened the meeting with brief introductions.

McDonald welcomed the group, calling them "an incredible group of young people."

Eileen Flint, of the city then gave a presentation on the need for citizen input as the city develops its new comprehensive plan, the long-range document that guides growth and development. Students were asked what they would like to see in Alamogordo's future.

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, former acting city manager, served as meeting facilitator after Flint's presentation. She told the students the commission will follow the New Mexico Open Meetings Act and walked them through a few basic procedures from Robert's Rules of Order.

The students put those rules to use right away. One of their first motions was to hold elections for the commission's executive members at the next meeting rather than at this one.

While mentors and staff asked occasional questions, the students did not hesitate to raise issues or ask questions of their own. Hernandez took notes as they spoke, and at least a couple of items are already set for the next agenda.

When asked what they hoped to gain from MYAC, students cited leadership, public speaking, and learning how city government works and how decisions are made.

When asked about their concerns, safety came first. Students raised safety for young drivers on city streets, substance abuse in schools and consequences for those who supply substances to children. They also discussed the need for safe places where young people can study, socialize and spend time after school, noting that not every student has the same home environment. The group had already begun talking about obstacles, including funding and how to make existing spaces safer.

"What impressed me most was that not one student approached the conversation from a selfish perspective," McDonald said. "They were advocating for their classmates, younger students, and people they may never meet."

McDonald said the commission is meant to put students in the lead.

"This isn't about adults telling kids what to do or deciding what matters to them. It's about kids telling adults what matters to THEM," she said. "Our role as mentors is to provide guidance, resources, and support, not dictate their priorities."

Near the end of the meeting, one student asked, "But how do we get people to listen to us?"

McDonald said the question both hurt and encouraged her.

"It hurts knowing some of our young people feel unheard, but it gives me tremendous hope that they WANT to participate," she said. "We often say our children are our future. But they are also our citizens TODAY."

As one mentor noted, first meetings are always a little awkward and slow. But conversations have already started among students and between students, the mayor and city staff about youth issues and possible projects. The future is bright with youth engagement and all left optimistic about a new voice being heard at city hall.

item.title: 2nd Life Media AlamogordoTownNews.org and KALHRadio.org Release Free Nonpartisan Otero County Voter Guide for the Nov. 3 Election
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M., Oct. 20, 2026 — With early voting under way and Election Day two weeks off, 2nd Life Media has published the 2026 Otero County Nonpartisan Voter Guide, a free 32-page reference that walks voters through every contest and every question on the county’s Nov. 3 general-election ballot. The guide is a joint project of AlamogordoTownNews.org and KALHRadio.org, with New Mexico Conservative News and The 47th Voice as partners.

The guide is available now as a free pdf download at:

https://drive.google.com/file/d/15T7BLUbtTV_4abE6xiCmFr8K-FZF6U5W/view?…

Otero County voters will decide 33 separate items this year, from the U.S. Senate to the county probate judge, plus four proposed amendments to the New Mexico Constitution and three statewide bond questions. The guide organizes all of them in ballot order and, for every contested race, gives each candidate the same treatment: a background sketch, a summary of where the candidate stands in the candidate’s own words, and a section reporting what opponents and critics say. Each constitutional amendment and bond question gets a plain-English explanation, a side-by-side table of the arguments for and against, and a list of who is publicly supporting and opposing it.

“Every race. Every question. Both sides.” is the guide’s stated standard. The publishers do not endorse any candidate or ballot question in it. Candidate positions are drawn from the candidates’ own campaign materials, questionnaires, debates and interviews; criticisms are attributed to the opponents and organizations making them, so readers can judge the source for themselves.

What’s inside

• Federal: U.S. Senate (Ben Ray Luján vs. Larry Marker) and the 2nd Congressional District (Gabriel Vasquez vs. Greg Cunningham).

• Statewide: Governor and Lieutenant Governor (Haaland/Garcia Richard vs. Hull/Gallegos), Secretary of State, Attorney General, State Auditor, State Treasurer and Commissioner of Public Lands.

• Judicial: the Court of Appeals special election and yes/no retention votes on two Supreme Court justices, a Court of Appeals judge and two 12th Judicial District judges, with the Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission’s recommendation on each.

• Legislature: the Senate District 33 special election and House Districts 51, 53, 54 and 56.

• County: County Commission Districts 1 and 2, Sheriff, Assessor, Probate Judge, both Magistrate divisions and Public Education Commission District 7.

• Constitutional Amendments 1–4: ending the governor’s pocket veto, allowing school elections alongside partisan elections, nominating committees for university regents, and a salary for state legislators tied to median household income.

item.title: A day after quitting the GOP, Zac Anaya says no one in either party is off limits
item.description:
RIO RANCHO — One day after announcing he had left the Republican Party, former GOP chair hopeful Zac Anaya said in a live interview Tuesday with Anthony Lucero that leaving the party has freed him to go after elected officials in both parties — including fellow conservatives he says he once went easy on.

"Independent doesn't mean I'm no longer a conservative," Anaya said. "It means that I'm able to vocalize my conservative values more than I would as a member of the Republican Party."

The 33-year-old Rio Rancho businessman announced Monday evening on social media that he had given up on the Republican Party of New Mexico and would register as an independent, 15 days before the Nov. 3 general election. In the live interview with host Anthony, he expanded on that post, took aim at party insiders over the governor's race and left the door open to returning — if the party changes its leadership.

In Monday's post, Anaya wrote that one of the most qualified Republicans to seek the governorship in a generation was struggling to raise money, without naming him. On Tuesday he named him: GOP nominee Gregg Hull, whom Anaya called "my mayor."

Anaya called Hull the most overqualified Republican gubernatorial candidate in at least 20 years and sharply criticized his Democratic opponent, Deb Haaland. He blamed Hull's fundraising gap on party insiders who he said resist Hull's "common sense ideas."

"They might do it on social media, but they're not doing it at a statewide monetary level," Anaya said of Republican support for Hull.

He went further, predicting Hull would lose by 11 points or more. "I hate to say that because I love Greg," he said.

The fundraising gap Anaya pointed to is real. Haaland remains well ahead in money according to reports filed Oct. 13. Hull raised about $634,000 in the latest period and roughly $1.5 million for the general election. His campaign has said the numbers reflect a focus on in-state donors — 99% of his donors are New Mexicans — and has cited donor fatigue after the June primary.

Anaya said that as an independent he would keep publishing political commentary and that officials of both parties are now fair game.

"If you're taking money, if you're married to a lobbyist, if you are making questionable votes, it's time to go after you," he said.

That line echoes his House District 60 primary campaign against state Rep. Joshua Hernandez (R-Rio Rancho), which Anaya lost in June. During that race Anaya filed a State Ethics Commission complaint accusing Hernandez of failing to disclose the lobbying clients of his partner and business associate; Hernandez called it a political stunt.

Anaya said Tuesday that Republican leaders, including Gail Armstrong and Rebecca Dow, called him during the primary and urged him to "leave Josh alone," and that he eased off as a result. He said Hernandez was one of five Republicans who voted for the universal child care bill, which Anaya later challenged in a lawsuit that the New Mexico Supreme Court rejected in July.

"That's not happening anymore," he said. "If you are corrupt, if you are making horrible votes, we're coming after you."

As 2nd Life Media reported Monday, Anaya's exit is the latest fallout from the yearlong fight over former party chair Amy Barela, who was removed by a court in May. Anaya briefly ran to replace her in June as part of the northern bloc opposing her, then stepped aside to avoid splitting that vote.

Anaya did not mention Barela by name Tuesday. But his conditions for coming back line up with the leadership question still hanging over the party, which enters the election under interim chair Mike Nelson and is set to pick a permanent chair after Nov. 3.

Anaya predicted a "reckoning" for Republicans after the election. "If the party can right itself with a proper chairperson and a new platform, then I may very well come back," he said.

Anaya said he left the Democratic Party after college because it had gone "a little wacko" and now sees Republicans doing the same — campaigning on conservative values and abandoning them in office. "At the end of the day, they love to spend our money," he said.

He described both parties as captured by their extremes, citing gender-related medical care for minors on the left and treating everything President Donald Trump says as "gospel truth" on the right. Most Americans, he said, sit somewhere in between.

He argued that Ronald Reagan and John F. Kennedy would both belong to the Forward Party today.

The host, KALHRadio.org’s Anthony Lucero for streaming Alamogordo Town News, compared Anaya's move to that of former Las Cruces Mayor Ken Miyagishima, who he said had voiced similar frustrations with the Democratic Party and endorsed Hull.

Anaya said he plans to spend more time with his wife, children and faith — a theme from Monday's post — while publishing opinion pieces on his website, zacanaya.com, and social media. 

He said he submits columns to newspapers across the state but that they have not run them. He has been extended an invitation to submit articles to us going forward. 

He closed by drawing on his recovery from addiction, which he has discussed publicly. 

"As somebody who is in recovery, I've learned that you have to admit the mistakes that you've made, admit that you're powerless, and surrender to a higher power," he said. "No politician is going to save you, no political party is going to save you."

item.title: Fact Check: John Block Sends Attack Letter: Relies on Insinuations and Falsehoods While Ignoring His Own Record of Division and Limited Results
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO  N.M. — In the closing weeks of the House District 51 campaign, Republican incumbent Rep. John Block mailed voters a two-page fundraising letter dated October 12, 2026. Rather than running primarily on a documented record of successful representation for Alamogordo and Otero County, the letter spends the bulk of its space attacking independent challenger Grace Nagamine with claims that public records, campaign finance filings, legislative documents, and her own disclosures contradict or leave without support

The letter portrays Nagamine as a Biden campaigner who “even met him,” a Harris supporter, a stand-in for an unnamed “far-left PAC” that has raised more than $300,000, an independent “the way Bernie Sanders is” who will caucus with Democrats the moment she reaches Santa Fe, and a “career criminal” whose record of “at least three felony convictions and other charges stretching over decades” disqualifies her

It contrasts this with Block’s assertion that he has delivered more than $11 million, kept promises on veterans and military families, and fought taxes and the shuttering of an ICE facility.

A review of New Mexico legislative records, Secretary of State campaign finance disclosures, court records, White House documents provided by the Nagamine campaign, and prior reporting shows the central attacks are unsupported or misleading. 

The letter also omits context that undercuts its framing, while overstating Block’s legislative achievements.

It arrives against a backdrop in which Block has faced public accusations from the state’s top election official of encouraging online harassment, maintains an active civil lawsuit set for trial after Election Day, and has used his own PAC structure in ways that route money involving his private company.

The “Career Criminal” Claim and the Record of Service

Block’s letter states that Nagamine’s record “includes at least three felony convictions and other charges stretching over decades for some of the most grievous crimes” and that this is “a career criminal’s record, not a public servant’s.”

According to Nagamine’s campaign and her published memoir, the convictions and related incarceration occurred in 2005–2008, tied to a period of domestic violence survival, addiction, and homelessness.

She has not disputed nor denied the existence of the record; she has described it publicly in her book The Grace Nagamine Story, in interviews, on social media, and as keynote speaker at a recent domestic violence survivors’ event.

Court-record reviews cited in local reporting have found no criminal cases against her in the roughly 18 years since.

The letter’s phrase “stretching over decades” does not match a record confined to a three-year period that ended nearly two decades ago.

The letter also omits the subsequent record of service.

White House letters provided by the Nagamine campaign document recognition under both parties through the President’s Volunteer Service Award program, which honors volunteer hours rather than political activity.

One letter signed by President Donald Trump congratulates her on the President’s Volunteer Service Award and thanks her for service to fellow Americans and those most in need.

A second letter signed by President Joe Biden presents the President’s Lifetime Achievement Award “in recognition of your 4,311 hours of service to this great Nation.” 

Nagamine has said that when she met Biden she brought her children so they could meet a sitting president, and that she would want them to show the same respect to any president regardless of party

Meeting a president and receiving volunteer recognition from two presidents is not campaigning nor politicking for either of them. 

The Block attack letter mentions the Biden meeting but not the Trump recognition.

Nagamine is a lifelong Alamogordo resident, former Mrs. New Mexico (2018–2019), founder of Royal Angels (a charity focused on children with special needs, established in honor of a granddaughter), a mother and grandmother, and an advocate for women, children, seniors, veterans, and survivors.

Her publicly stated platform centers on local issues including veterans and Holloman AFB, seniors and caregivers, children and CYFD reform, homelessness, and infrastructure. 

She has described running as a Decline to State (Independent) candidate because these problems do not belong to one party and has spoken of the need for bipartisan collaboration.

Unsupported Claims on Politics, Caucusing, and Outside Money

The letter calls Nagamine independent “the way Bernie Sanders is,” asserts she is “ready to caucus with” Democrats the moment she reaches Santa Fe, and claims she supported Kamala Harris’s 2024 campaign.

It cites no statement from her pledging to caucus with Democrats, no public endorsement of Harris, and no donation record. 

Federal contributions are public via FEC filings; none supporting the Harris claim has been identified in available reporting.

Nagamine filed as a Decline to State candidate; her materials state she is not affiliated with any political party. No public record of a pledge to join the Democratic caucus nor any caucus has been located.

The letter further claims she is “backed by a far-left PAC that has raised over $300,000 and is now spending it to support Democrats down the ballot and flip our district blue.

It does not name the PAC. Nagamine’s state campaign finance reports through mid-2026 showed no PAC contributions of that scale. She has received a Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter endorsement based on her local knowledge and community work; an endorsement is not a $300,000 contribution. Available independent expenditures supporting her have been described as modest grassroots efforts. The claim lacks supporting documentation.

By contrast, Block’s own campaign reports list contributions from Chevron, Permian Resources, Devon Energy, and other corporate and out-of-district sources. Piñon PAC, of which Block is treasurer and which shares an address with his Piñon Post LLC, has raised tens of thousands of dollars, the large majority from Republican legislators outside Otero County. Filings show the PAC paid Piñon Post LLC more than $4,600 in 2026 with no purpose disclosed beyond generic descriptions such as “Check.” Money has also moved between Block’s campaign committee, the PAC, and Block personally.

Fact: The Block letter warns that “outside money does not knock on doors,” yet Block’s own filings show substantial outside support while local Otero County contributions to the PAC have been minimal.

Overstated Claims About Block’s Legislative Record

The letter credits Block with bringing home more than $11 million for Alamogordo and Otero County. Every House member receives an equal share of capital outlay funds, roughly $2.5 million annually; four years of that standard allocation is approximately $10 million.

Local fact-checks have noted that Block voted against the 2026 capital outlay reauthorization and the state budget. In the 2026 session, four of the 37 measures he sponsored passed, and he was not the lead sponsor on any of them and ranks in the bottom 1/3 of his own Republican Caucus for effectiveness even surpassed by a first term novice Republican for effectiveness. 

He claims he “helped pass increased property tax relief for our veterans.” The veterans’ property-tax bills that became law (including HB 47 in 2025 and HB 285 in 2026) were sponsored by other legislators; HB 285 passed the House 67–0. He states he “passed bills to make it easier for military families.” He was one of five co-sponsors, not the lead sponsor, of HB 302 (2024), which added protections for military families.

He claims he fought “attempts to raise our taxes by trying to shutter our ICE detention facility.” HB 9 (2026) bars counties from ICE detention contracts, putting the Otero County Processing Center’s jobs and revenue at risk; it does not raise taxes, and lawmakers set aside funds to offset county losses

Fact: These claims range from inflated to partly true to misleading when measured against the legislative record.

Pattern of Division Versus Collaboration

While Nagamine has emphasized bipartisan approaches to local problems and has been recognized for service by presidents of both parties, Block’s public record includes sharp partisan attacks.

In November 2024, New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver publicly accused Block of encouraging or “egging on” online harassment and threats she received after the election, including during a legislative committee hearing.

She indicated she planned to file a police report related to intimidation of election officials. Block denied threatening or harassing her, offered a qualified apology for any violent threats directed at her, and characterized questions about her policy positions as legitimate debate.  The episode is documented in contemporaneous reporting by the Albuquerque Journal, Santa Fe New Mexican, and Associated Press.

Block has also been a frequent critic of Democratic leadership, including filing ethics complaints and using his Piñon Post platform for pointed commentary.

Separately, he is a defendant in an ongoing LBGTQ civil lawsuit filed by his former domestic partner, over a property agreement; a judge has set the case for a multi-day trial beginning in March 2027. 

Block threatened a defamation lawsuit and previously told constituents the matter had been resolved amicably; court orders show it was not. A State Ethics Commission complaint involving related matters was also filed against him. .

New Mexico law requires clear disclaimers on campaign advertising identifying who authorized and paid for it. The letter reviewed carries Block’s campaign branding and lists an address for checks but does not display a boxed statement of authorization and payment of the campaign materials in the manner described under state statute and rules. Whether that complies is a question for the State Ethics Commission and the SOS of which is investigating. 

Conclusion

Block’s letter asks voters to judge character and trust “neighbors.

On the claims that can be checked against public records, Nagamine’s history of service is documented by volunteer awards from both President Trump and President Biden.

Her criminal record is real, old, self-disclosed, and followed by years of clean time and community work.

The letter’s characterizations of her politics, funding, and caucus intentions lack supporting evidence.

Block’s own claims about delivering uniquely for the district are inflated relative to the shared capital outlay process and the legislative record of co-sponsorship rather than sole authorship.

The Block letter continues a pattern of attacking an opponent through insinuation rather than resting the case primarily on a clear, unvarnished record of results for District 51.

item.title: 'Easy to be a Monday morning quarterback': Dr Hernandez answers critics of city projects
item.description:
Alamogordo NM -Alamogordo's former interim city manager Dr Stephanie Hernandez is pushing back against recent criticism of four city infrastructure projects, arguing that critics are judging past decisions without knowing the circumstances behind them.

"It's easy to be a Monday morning quarterback," Hernandez said in recorded remarks. "I worked under city managers, and I would never criticize the decisions because I don't know all the circumstances they faced."

The four projects — the Oregon Avenue project, the Great Blocks New York Ave he project, the fire station and the 10th Street Bridge — were recently criticized during a public meeting. Hernandez said three of them dated back to 2022, under former City Manager Brian Cesar. Since then, the city's top administrative job passed from Cesar to Hernandez, to Rick Holden, and back to Hernandez.

"These projects were already designed," she said. "Much of the funding came from grants with deadlines. Further delays risk the projects altogether."

Hear in her own words:

Hernandez said the Great Blocks project was backed by millions of dollars in state money and went through three change orders, including a pedestrian improvement added in response to public feedback that fell "completely outside the original scope." She noted the project later received an award from the state and she as also recognized by the state for excellence in collaborations with the State MainStreet organization.

The fire station, she said, went through three fire chiefs and several changes. Chief Ramirez wanted the project's funding used to improve response times on the city's south side, and the city got that funding reauthorized.

On Oregon Avenue, Hernandez said new infrastructure that was not part of the original design was added so the street would not have to be torn up later. The commission approved two change orders on that project. Hernandez said she questioned a later extension, but it "was approved without much discussion."

The 10th Street Bridge was found to have structural problems, and a permanent fix required more engineering, time and money, she said. Hernandez said Commissioners Rardin and Guthrie pushed hard to reopen the street without a permanent solution, while Hernandez and Rardin criticized the inconvenience. Staff worked on another temporary fix while designing a longer-term Washington canal project, with 10th Street as its first phase.

Hernandez said the four projects did not reflect the city's full record. About 20 other projects were completed, she said, including the Hubbard Bridge — a problem she remembered from childhood — which was finished in roughly three months.

She said several other projects have completed designs from the same engineering firms whose work is now being re-reviewed, and that she tracked every project and still has records showing where each stood when she left. Projects such as Oregon WSRP phases two and three should be moving forward, she said. She had wanted one underway during the summer to minimize disruption around the school administration building, and the Alaska section finished before Christmas because of increased traffic to the post office.

But knowing she was leaving, Hernandez said, she chose not to start those projects. "I respected the incoming city manager enough not to start projects and tie his hands."

Hernandez acknowledged she was not satisfied with how every project was handled. She said she was vocal about contractor delays, which at times put her at odds with contractors and commissioners, and that the city was already working toward better, fairer processes.

"There's a difference between improving and waiting for perfection," she said. "Anyone who's remodeled a home with the best plans and contractors knows that problems are going to happen. You address them and move on."

She warned against letting projects sit while funding opportunities expire.

"Citizens don't benefit from projects sitting on paper; they benefit when projects get completed," Hernandez said. "And Alamogordo deserves progress."

item.title: Presumptive Sheriff Elect Geraldine Yazza Martinez Shares Halloween Safety Tips
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — With Halloween just around the corner, Geraldine Yazza Martinez, the Republican candidate for Otero County Sheriff, is reminding families to keep safety in mind as trick-or-treaters head out across the county.

In her own words:

In a message to the community, Martinez addressed "all the little goblins, ghouls, princesses, superheroes, and accompanying adults" who will be out knocking on doors and traveling through neighborhoods on Halloween night.

Her first piece of advice was aimed at parents: "Adults, supervise your kids." For older children going out without parents, she recommended the buddy system and carrying a flashlight.

Martinez urged trick-or-treaters to use sidewalks or paths and to cross only at corners and designated crosswalks. She also stressed making eye contact with drivers before stepping into the road, "that you know they see you."

"As always, and most importantly, stay sober," Martinez said. "No drinking and driving."

She closed on a lighter note, telling kids not to eat too much candy — "at least not until your parents have had a chance to check it out first."

"We want everyone to have a fun, safe Halloween," she said.

item.title: Tularosa trustees delay vote on 190-foot cell tower after residents pack hearing
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — The Tularosa Board of Trustees heard more than an hour of testimony Monday on a proposed 190-foot cell tower at 44 Sunset Road, and then put off its decision. Most of the testimony came from residents who oppose the project. The board will vote at a special meeting that has not been scheduled yet.

"I don't like to make this like quick decision," the mayor said at the end of the Oct. 19 special meeting. "I want to look at everything, look it over, take considerations in before we make that quick decision." The trustees agreed.

The village attorney, speaking by phone, told the board the item had been noticed properly and it could have acted that night. She also said the vote could not go on the board's regular meeting this Wednesday because there was not enough time to put it on the agenda.

The application

Flagship One LLC is asking for a special use permit, case 2026 SUP 002, to build a wireless tower on a parcel of about 15 acres behind a home. The applicant's representative, Sean Milks, said the parcel needed its own address for the tower. The hearing was quasi-judicial, which means trustees were reviewing the record built by the Planning and Zoning Commission. That commission adopted findings of fact on Sept. 8.

Shannon Naysenzer of Planning and Zoning told the board the commission does not recommend approval or denial of special use permits. It does recommend 12 conditions that Flagship One would have to meet before getting a building permit. They include:

Flagship One has also agreed to reserve a spot on the tower, at 150 feet or lower, for village and emergency equipment at nominal cost.

Milks joined by phone after about 15 minutes of audio problems. He said the company now proposes a monopole instead of a three-legged lattice tower. A monopole is 70% to 75% smaller in diameter and costs more to build, he said. He also said it is designed to fold onto itself in sections instead of falling over, and that it will not carry a light.

"I know we upset people from time to time," Milks said. "We're trying to do a happy medium, which is another reason I opted to offer to make the [pole] significantly smaller."

He said his company has built 46 sites in New Mexico, and 30 to 35 of them sit close to homes. He said he had never seen or heard of a tower falling in the state in his 29 years in the business.

Setbacks dispute

The sharpest exchanges were about the fall zone. Eva J. Gonzalez asked whether the tower meets the setback, the tower's height plus 10%, on all four sides of the property. Milks said it meets three. In cases like this, he said, the company submits an extra analysis from a New Mexico licensed engineer certifying that the pole and foundation are over-engineered.

"I'm telling you under oath, the pole will not fall down," Milks said.

"And I'm telling you under oath that you cannot guarantee anything like that," Gonzalez replied.

David Gonzalez, of Cortez Drive, said county assessor records put the parcel at 362 feet wide. By his math, a 190-foot tower plus 10 feet on each side would need 400. He also said the application includes drawings dated August 2018 that refer to Raglan, New Mexico. He listed five different tower heights in the paperwork, up to 203 feet, and said the federal antenna registration still describes a lattice tower. "Why are we even looking at this application if all this information is wrong?" he asked. The mayor ended his comments when his five minutes ran out.

Naysenzer said the main application does list Tularosa and that the permit is preliminary. The village attorney said the commission's findings clearly describe a 190-foot tower with a one-to-one fall zone. She added that trustees could make the monopole design a condition of approval.

Coverage, petition and alternatives

Eva Gonzalez cited CarrierLytics, an analytics platform that uses FCC coverage maps. It shows T-Mobile coverage at 98.6% and Verizon at 98.3% in the 88352 ZIP code. "There is no significant gap in coverage warranting the installation of another cell tower in the village," she said. She then submitted a petition with 198 signatures from Tularosa residents asking the board to deny the permit. Milks answered that capacity, not just coverage, is driving new sites, and that the carriers have signed a 30-year lease.

Several speakers suggested other sites. Frank Portillo said a landowner east of the site has a small range of hills that could hold a shorter tower out of residents' direct view, and wants to talk with the company. Milks said the project had already gone too far through surveys and reviews to start over. Kevin Ferguson asked about land the village plans to buy. The mayor said the village cannot offer land it does not own yet.

Billy Hobson questioned whether a personal relationship with the property owner influenced where the tower would go. Milks said the site was chosen from a search area set by a radio-frequency engineer.

Other residents talked about Tularosa's place on the National Register of Historic Places, their mountain views and home values. "We don't have high rises. We don't have skyscrapers. We don't need a cell phone tower here," said Denise Ottaviano, whose mother lives on Cortez Drive. Juan A. Osorio raised health concerns. Before testimony began, the mayor had reminded the audience that the federal Telecommunications Act of 1996 bars local governments from denying a tower over radio-frequency health concerns if it meets FCC standards.

Larry Berry asked what happens to the removal bond if the company goes bankrupt. Milks said FCC rules require the owner to take the tower down if no carrier broadcasts from it for six straight months. He said the bond is paid up front and stays tied to the tower.

Village staff said they sent 49 certified notices to nearby property owners, reaching farther than the required distance. Six were not picked up.

item.title: Judge Orders Meta to Pay $25 Billion in New Mexico Deception Case
item.description:
SANTA FE, N.M. — A New Mexico judge on Wednesday ordered Meta Platforms Inc. to pay a $25 billion civil penalty, concluding that the company formerly known as Facebook spent more than a decade misleading the public about how it handled users' data, policed misinformation and hate speech, and enforced its own rules.

First Judicial District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew found that the state was entitled to $219.5 billion under the maximum penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act — $5,000 for each of 43,899,720 violations found by a jury — before reducing the award to $25 billion. The judgment, filed at 10:51 a.m., also orders interest to accrue at 15% a year until the penalty is paid in full. At that rate, interest alone would amount to roughly $3.75 billion a year.

The order does not explain how the court arrived at the $25 billion figure. The judge reserved a decision on injunctive relief, which could require changes to Meta's practices, pending further briefing.

The case, State of New Mexico ex rel. Raúl Torrez v. Meta Platforms, Inc., was filed in 2021 and decided after a 13-day trial before a 12-person jury.

Jurors found 26 public statements by Facebook and its executives to be unlawful and willful. The statements were made between May 24, 2010, and Aug. 18, 2021, through Facebook's own newsroom, earnings calls, national television and print interviews, and public conferences. Some were made personally by CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former COO Sheryl Sandberg.

The statements fell into five areas:

The violation counts came from the jury's estimate of each statement's audience in New Mexico. For each statement, jurors used either 1,386,648 — Facebook's New Mexico monthly active users as of mid-2020 — or 2,100,000, roughly the state's entire population. The jury also found five separate willful violations for unconscionable trade practices, one in each subject area.

Much of the judgment focuses on what Facebook said after the Cambridge Analytica scandal broke in March 2018. The company publicly pledged to investigate every app with large-scale access to user data, audit suspicious apps, ban developers who misused data, make sure improperly obtained data was deleted, and notify every affected user.

The court found Facebook knew at the time it could not keep those promises because of poor record-keeping and lax vetting of developers. Over the three-year investigation, the company conducted only 14 forensic "audits," despite thousands of apps showing suspicious activity. It notified users about just two apps, after deliberately narrowing its internal definition of "misuse" to limit the burden of notification, the judge wrote.

Facebook linked 1,585 of the more than 2,000 problem apps identified at trial to New Mexico accounts, affecting at least 1,146,225 state residents — more than 80% of its New Mexico users. The investigation ended in March 2021 without a public announcement, even though an internal legal review in September 2019 concluded the company could not say it had met its commitments.

The judge also cited a Sandberg email sent to advisers shortly after the scandal broke, warning that a "MILLION developers" had access to the data.

The court separately found that, more than a year before Facebook announced in 2014 that it was ending "friend sharing," the company was already planning undisclosed exemptions for favored business partners.

The judgment quotes a private Zuckerberg email in which he wrote that users "probably don't understand their current privacy settings," and outlined a plan to make more information public without encouraging users to change their settings. The court found Zuckerberg chose to exploit that confusion to help Facebook compete with Twitter.

On content moderation, the court found that Facebook's internal research showed its systems recommended groups and pages containing known misinformation, and that its "CrossCheck" program let content from celebrities, business partners and other high-profile accounts stay up while under extended review — about 12 days on average for U.S. accounts, according to the Oversight Board. The judge quoted a 2020 document in which integrity chief Guy Rosen acknowledged that the company was effectively delaying enforcement against violating content from those accounts.

Judge Mathew wrote that the number of violations, their duration, the involvement of senior leadership and the "clearly intentional and systematic" nature of the conduct supported the highest penalty allowed under state law.

The court rejected Meta's argument that its $5 billion settlement with the Federal Trade Commission should weigh against a large penalty, finding that prior penalties and consent decrees "have not deterred Meta." It also noted that the U.S. Supreme Court has not held that the Eighth Amendment's ban on excessive fines applies to corporations.

The judgment cites Meta's 2025 annual report, which listed revenue of nearly $201 billion and stockholders' equity of about $217 billion. The $25 billion penalty equals roughly one-eighth of a year's revenue.

This is Meta's second major trial loss in Santa Fe this year. In March, a separate jury in a 2023 lawsuit brought by Attorney General Raúl Torrez ordered Meta to pay $375 million after finding the company misled the public about child safety on Facebook and Instagram. Meta said it would appeal that verdict.

Meta's response to Wednesday's judgment was not immediately available.
